title: Uptown BIA levy and heritage housing grant request
subtitle: University of Waterloo presentation, Enova board nominees, Rogers antenna and Button Factory licences, Erb Street West by-laws.
overview: Council set the 2026 Uptown Waterloo Business Improvement Area levy at $806,195 {{vote:m4}}. The levy funds the BIA's operating and capital costs, including events, cleaning and beautification work in the Uptown core. Council also asked the Mayor to write to the Premier and other provincial officials supporting a proposed provincial Heritage Helping Housing Building Grant {{vote:m6}}. The grant would help owners convert older and heritage buildings into housing.

On the consent agenda, council approved an amendment to the Rogers Communications antenna licence at 265 Lexington Court {{vote:m2}} and a licence renewal with Button Factory Arts for 25 Regina St S {{vote:m3}}. It also approved new terms for two City-nominated independent directors on the Enova Energy Corporation board {{vote:m5}}.

Council heard a University of Waterloo presentation on the university's economic impact. It also passed by-laws giving effect to Erb Street West official plan and zoning changes that council approved on March 23. Council met in closed session on drinking water infrastructure; the minutes report no decisions from it.

decisions.detail: Council approved the Uptown Waterloo BIA's 2026 special levy of $806,195 and the by-law imposing it on rateable properties in the BIA.

Council asked the Mayor to write to the Premier and other provincial officials requesting that Ontario create the grant proposed by Architectural Conservancy Ontario, and to share the resolution with area MPPs and heads of council.
Council approved successive terms for David Petras, until the 2028 Enova AGM, and Tim Martin, until the 2027 AGM, as City-nominated independent directors.
Council approved an amendment to the Rogers Communications antenna licence at 265 Lexington Court and authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign it.
Council approved a licence agreement with Button Factory Arts for use of the building at 25 Regina St S and authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign it.

debate: On the BIA levy, a councillor asked why the levy was rising when the BIA's operating spending was falling. The BIA's executive director said federal and provincial grants for placemaking projects have ended, so the BIA is focusing on basics such as cleaning, beautification and activation.

On beautification, the BIA's executive director described cost-sharing with the City. The BIA contributes to the floral program, Sunday waste pickup and summer sidewalk sweeping. Staff and the BIA said Uptown needs to stay clean and attractive to keep businesses and talent.

A delegate for Architectural Conservancy Ontario argued that reusing heritage buildings for housing can be faster, cheaper and more sustainable than new construction. The delegate also said it is more labour-intensive, which means more local jobs. The proposed grant would cover half of eligible costs up to a cap per unit.

Councillors supporting the heritage motion said current incentives for heritage projects are weak. They pointed to places of worship that could be redeveloped and to housing conversions elsewhere in Canada as examples. The delegate said there is no firm provincial timeline, and the grant would likely be considered in next year's budget.

After the University of Waterloo presentation, councillors asked how to keep talent and companies in the city given the venture funding gap and the lack of new commercial space. They also asked how to better tell the story of the university's research partnerships with the City. The university representative pointed to the regional AI coalition and co-op students.
